Hip-to-Gable Loft Conversion in Barnet

A hip-to-gable loft conversion in Barnet is the classic way to transform a 1920s or 1930s semi in Edgware, Mill Hill, Hendon or Finchley. Barnet has more of these hipped-roof houses than almost anywhere in London, and on many streets a converted gable is now the norm.

  • Edgware, Mill Hill, Hendon, Finchley and Burnt Oak
  • Often permitted development
  • Usually combined with a rear dormer

Local knowledge

Barnet's Interwar Semis and Their Hipped Roofs

When the Northern line reached Edgware in 1924, the fields of north-west Barnet were sold off plot by plot to speculative builders, and within a decade Edgware, Burnt Oak, Mill Hill and Hendon were covered in semi-detached houses.1 Almost all have hipped roofs, which leave the loft narrow at the side. Squaring off that side with a gable, and usually adding a rear dormer, turns it into a full-width room with space for a staircase.

Because so many pairs have been converted, a hip-to-gable often fits the established character of a Barnet street. Where planning permission is needed, Barnet's 2016 Residential Design Guidance asks that the gable should not appear out of character, a test planning inspectors have applied at appeal.2 On a street where neighbouring pairs already have gables, that is a far easier case to make. Detached houses in Mill Hill and Totteridge can have hips on both sides, and converting both gives the largest loft of all, though it uses up more of the 50 cubic metre allowance.

Planning in Barnet

Planning a Hip-to-Gable in Barnet

  • Permitted development: within 50 cubic metres on a semi or detached house, exempt from the 20 cm eaves set-back. Barnet has issued lawful development certificates for hip-to-gable and rear dormer schemes.3, 4
  • Planning application: judged on whether the gable looks out of character with the street.
  • Hampstead Garden Suburb and other Article 4 areas: roof alterations need planning permission.

Interwar Barnet semis usually have rendered or pebble-dashed upper walls and plain clay or concrete tiles. We finish the new gable to match, so it reads as part of the original house rather than an addition.

FAQ

Barnet Hip-to-Gable FAQs

Is a hip-to-gable permitted development in Barnet?

Often, yes, on a semi-detached or detached house outside conservation areas and Article 4 areas, within 50 cubic metres and below the existing ridge. Barnet regularly issues lawful development certificates for hip-to-gable and rear dormer schemes.

How does Barnet judge a hip-to-gable that needs planning?

Against its 2016 Residential Design Guidance. Planning inspectors have quoted its requirement that the gable should not appear out of character, which in practice means looking at whether other houses on the street have been converted and how your pair would look.

Will I need a party wall notice for a hip-to-gable in Barnet?

On a semi-detached house, usually yes. The new steels typically bear onto the wall shared with your neighbour, which needs at least two months' notice under the Party Wall etc. Act 1996.
